blocks.x: Joseph Watkins Okay, it's going. Do you want to give your name?
All right. My name is Joseph Watkins. I'm drumming with the George Lewis jazz band. At the present time, been waiting for about 12 or 13 years.
Give your birth date too.
Yeah, well my birth date is October 24th, 1900. 59 this coming October, I'll be 60, God's bad life, and I'll live to see it.
Were you born right in the city?

Yeah, born in red right here in New Orleans. Only time I've been out of town is when the George Lewis band had trips away. And we've been very successful so far, so good, and I hope we continue to be that way until some of us start pegging out. And I started playing drums back in 1923.
Had you played any other instruments first? Any like guitar? No, no other instruments.
I was just crazy about drums from a child when Baby Dots was playing in New Orleans at that time. Baby Dots, Henry Martin, Black Benny, Two Bits, and all those drummers.
Well tell me, I don't want to interrupt you all the time, but tell me about Two Bits. I know Bunk used to mention Two Bits, and I never heard anybody else mention it until you did.

Well he's a little short, light, brown-skinned fella, except more than all the George Lewis. Well he used to play up a lot of drums, and we had a fella, another fella around there, we used to call a...
Do you know his real name, Two Bits?
No, all I knew was Two Bits.
I never did ask Bunk about him, but Bunk mentioned he'd been in a band at Pete Lala's one time. Yeah, that's what I heard.
Well I was practically a small kid. I was around in my teens then.
Did he come from uptown or downtown? Well no, I knew him from the Third Ward.
He was living on Howard between Perdita and Gravia, and I was living on... I mean, yeah, Perdita and Gravia. And I was living on Perdita between Howard and Liberty.
Were you born up that way?

I was born in Charity Hospital, and I was raised up on Ramport between Gerard and Julia. And we left from there, we moved to Perdita Street between Liberty and Howard. And from there we moved up to Carlton, and back down to the old Tenderline District a few years before they closed it up. Well I went to work around there when I was 13 years old, and Henry Martin was playing drums at Rice Cafe, right at the corner of Iberville and Murray. Right across the street from Pete Lollers. Well I don't know what band they had at that time at Pete Lollers, because I was too young to go in there, you know, and naturally I was getting by at my age, because I was the youngest bellhopper and waiter they had around in that time, around 1913. And naturally I had to put on long pants for my parents to keep me around there, so they put me to work and I went to work as a bellhop for Frederick Grouse. Well that was all big names, Frederick Grouse and...
Where was this place, what was it, the saloon?

Yeah, it was a bar and a barroom and a grocery. It was right at the corner of Liberty and Quarantine, right opposite the old St. Louis Street Cemetery. Oh yeah. And I worked there for a couple of years, and well we moved away from there, and I just forget now where the devil we moved to.
But that place you said, what street was it on, between St. Louis and Quarantine?

Right on the corner, at Liberty and Quarantine. Liberty, oh. Yeah, right on the corner, second catacomb from St. Louis Street Cemetery, yeah. Well I had the opportunity to get in to Lula White's place, and Emma Johnson and Willa Piazza, I used to deliver drinks to those different places, and naturally it was good money in them days, the salary wasn't much but the tips were so great, you know. Well I did fairly good, and I left from there, and right after they closed the district down in 1916 I think it was. And at that time George A. Fuller was building up the Port of Embarcation. I went to work down there for quite a while. Then I left from there, and I went to work up on Barone Street at a printing office. Well I had quite a little struggle there for a while, you know, before I had actually taken up more interest in music, because when I was a kid I used to go to old Kenny's Funky Butt Hall on Bedita, between Liberty and Franklin, and I used to watch Baby Dots, and Bunk was playing, used to play that too, I'm more than sure.
Probably did, yeah.

And I used to watch Baby Dots anytime when I got a chance to go hear them, and I used to watch Henry Martin, I watched Black Benny, and Red Happy, and all those fellas that was making a name for themselves. And, well I never did learn music, I just taken interest, so much interest in it that I fell in love with the drums and I'd taken them up.
When you were a kid, did you play on any toy drums or beat on anything?

No, no, no. I didn't beat on it. All I beat it on was the bottom of my mother's old wash tub or upside the fence, yeah. Yeah. So around 1918 I went to work at the Whitney National Bank as a night port. At that time they had Bud Russel, I know you know him. I've heard him. Ed Darcy was working there. Well Ed Darcy's still with him, yeah, but Bud Russel died. Well I was playing piano with a boyfriend of mine named Shedrick Brewster, but we called him nicknamed Baby Brewster, and we used to play house parties on Sundays. In fact we played practically all over town. Well I had bought me a brand new set of drums from Wordless I sent out to Chicago for him. And that's how I started getting the fundamentals of drums. I didn't have nobody to teach me. I wasn't able to pay nobody for a music lesson. Well Henry Martin he'd done the best he could for me when I was trying to learn, but he wasn't learning how to read. How did Henry Martin play?
What style? Was it something like Baby Dodds or anything particular about his style you could tell us?
Well I can't say it was any too close to Baby Dodds, but he was really a good jazz drummer in his days.
What kind of a drum set, can you remember what kind of a set he had? See he's not around naturally to tell us what-

Well in them days they had overhanging pedals. Yeah. And he had a cymbal, wood block, in those days they had their wood shell snare drums, and Chinese tum tum. But I never noticed what kind of a drum stand he was using.
Was it a big bass drum or small? What size?
No, pretty good sized bass drum. How big did they use in those days? Something on all of Baby Dodds bass drum I believe.
How big did they use in those days? Do you remember in-
Well I think it was around 28.

Yeah. I think it was a 28. And well I never did actually let me set in because I was kind of leery about setting in and you know in anybody's band or anything like that. So while we was living in Calton, Johnny Saint Seale was living up there at that time, well he used to play a little combo right at the corner from his house at Boydette and Hickory. He was living on Hickory between Boydette and Adams. Well he used to play there and he didn't have no drums handed so they had long benches and I used to have a pair of drumsticks and I used to sit on the side of the bench you know and pat my foot along with them keeping the tempo and beating on the bench you know. So he told me, he said, well you keep it up. He said, you'll probably get somewhere if you're really interested in it. Well after we moved back downtown and I started and I got my first set of drums, well he went to Chicago. When he went to play with Louie, I'm more sure he left to go play with Louie at that time, the first time he went to Chicago. Yeah. And after he left Louie he went with Professor Cook. I'm more sure that's the way it was, but I know that first was playing out here on the steam of Capitol.
Yes, he played with Faith Marable. Yeah, that's right, yeah, Faith Marable, yeah.

He played with them for several years and they left from there and he went on to Chicago. Well I knocked around different jobs with no particular bands and when Bud Russel came out and heard me one night, right a few blocks up here on Galvest Street on a Sunday night, brought his bass along. So that made us have three pieces and the boyfriend of ours used to play them kazooch. You could hardly tell if you was on about a couple blocks away you'd swear it was a trumpet.
Really?
Because he was short and fat and he had plenty of strong wind, strong lungs.
Is it something like the one that Noon has or different?
No, no, just one of them little short ones that you use.
Oh, the record kazoo, a little one.
The record kazooch that you use cigarette paper.
Yeah, sure.

And after he had heard me, he told me about joining up with him and Foster Lewis. Him and Foster, what they call him, Foster Stan. But it was Foster Stan and his brother dude had their own band. And so when they got jobs where we used to take off, you know, get off them nights and go play the job and come back and finish our work. So he told me, he gave me good advice. He said, you keep up. He said, you got a little, a little bit to learn yet. So after I got married, well, I had given up music because the depression that came along and things that got so tough. I said, well, I just said, well, to get rid of those set. I said, because they ain't nothing gonna happen for quite a long time. So we moved right across the street from here, right next to the church there, before they built the church up. A friend of mine named Walter Nelson, you done heard him, I'm more sure. Well, yes, I've heard of him.
He's still a guitar player.

Yeah, I never knew him. Well, we went up to Wilford's house, Wilford Ledet. He was a drummer. Well, he had a set of drums up there. Well, I wasn't worried about no drum. We was just sitting down and having a good time. And I started to pat my foot and Walter said, you ever played drums before? I said, yeah. I said, why, yeah? He said, well, I noticed you're keeping good time with your foot. I said, yeah, I used to play quite a while. And so Wilford set up his drums and it was him. And I and the guitar. So during that year for Halloween night, Wilford had got a job back in Gentilly. It was in a barn, cow barn. And he asked if I wanted to play the job. I said, well, I don't have no set. He said, well, I'll let you use my set. So it was Hubert Moran on trumpet, Walter Nelson on guitar and me on drums. So after we knocked off that night Hubert Moran told me, he said, Joe, I like your style of playing. So you kind of remind me of Lindsey a little bit. He said, why don't you get your set? And so we come around by your house and give you rehearsals and get you back in the racket again. You can make a little extra change. So I went and bought a secondhand outfit. And well, they used to come over there and hear me, Walter, just them two. And they used to work me out several times a week. And first thing you know, we had six pieces. Well, we started playing all down the country. And then we was playing out here by Joe Chenellis at the Silver Star.
Who else was in the band?
And well, at that time we had him see Walter Moran and this crippled fellow used to play clarinet. How did Walter play?
Guitar.

And we had a crippled fellow on the clarinet. I can't think of his name now. He's dead. And sometimes we have George Lewis and drag. Well, the piano player, I didn't know his name. Then we had another fellow by the name of Alfred used to play sax with us sometime when we couldn't get clarinet. Well, how I come to get into the George Lewis band, I played with Eddie Morris back at Linfans, back on Canal Boulevard. One Sunday afternoon. And George had a job at the corner from Drag's house. And he needed a drummer. So Drag told him about me, he said, well, go get him. He said, cause he's a good drummer. So Drag came and got me that night, left wood over at the house for a minute. So I went on a dead job with him that night. And the following week he had an advertisement for a prize fight. And he wanted to know if I could play that with him. I told him, yeah. So I played that with him, that night with him. And on the truck in the meantime he said, Joe, you playing with anybody regularly? I said, no, nobody but you all. He said, well, how would you like to work with me? He said, be able to make some good change. I said, sure. I said, I'll play with you until you can do better. Get somebody better, you know. Cause I didn't want him to think I was trying to be a hog or anything like that. So he said, alright. He said, you stick with me. He said, you're going to make it. He said, cause I like your style of playing. So you're playing that old time way. I said, well, alright. Well, we finally landed a job back on Benefit and St. Rock at Manny's. We played back there Friday and Saturday nights every week until the band started getting popular. And then we, Nick taking a liking to the band and he wanted to manage us. So George accepted him. And we went on out to El Moraca. That was around 1949 or 50, something like that. So from the El Moraca, that's where we started getting our breaks. Reverend Kershaw and Dr. Ball from Cincinnati. Where Reverend Kershaw was from Oxford. He had his church, Episcopal Church up there. And Dr. Ball was a professor at the University of Cincinnati. And they came down and they checked all the bands and they selected our band, the best one. So they started us to coming up into Cincinnati. And from Cincinnati, we started going out to Los Angeles. From Los Angeles, we started going into Frisco. And after that, we started going to several different states.
Well, somebody told me a few months ago, Reverend Kershaw was a professor. Did you ever hear any of them?
No.
I don't believe it's true.

No, because I got a letter from his secretary a week before last. Oh good, then he still. Yeah, you see, because I always write to her and she writes to me. And whenever she tell me he ain't too busy, well, I write to him.
Yeah.
You see, I got a card from him for Christmas. Well, I ain't heard from him since that.
Well, that's before that.

Well, she, you see, she told me that they had been very busy. Mm-hmm. And he had tried to get the band out there before George left, but I don't know, there was some misunderstanding between, with Miss Tate, I don't know what happened. But anyhow, Miss Tate wrote and told me that she wasn't any too optimistic about the job. Now, I don't know what the terms was about. So, I said, well, that's just a dead issue until they come back. So, I know, I'm more than sure when they come back why something will be worked out because the secretary wrote and told me that he's waiting on Miss Tate when she come back. She don't let him know why, for me to write and let him know when they get back. But anyway, to finish talking about George Lewis, I've been traveling all over with him. That's in the place I haven't been with him yet. Been overseas when they played here in America, practically every state in the union here. And, well, I'm expecting to hear some good news from him when they come back off of this trip because, you see, they trying to work up some deals while they're over there. Well, I'm more than sure because from the letters that I've been getting from over there, I think that's what's going to happen most likely to go back this summer.
Sure, they'd like to have the whole band.

Yeah, you see, but just like the band, I'm sure. Just like he said that they working this deal like they did before, bringing him over first and then bringing the band over afterwards, you know. So he was on the impression that his band was going to be broke up. I said, no, I said, as long as you got me in drag, your band will never be broke up. No. But I said, as far as getting another man, I said, I'm more than sure you can get somebody to replace Jim and Howard.
Yes, Jim doesn't want to travel much anymore.

Jim ain't particular about traveling too much and they tell me Howard is pretty sick so there's no need to try to rely on fellows like that to travel anywhere, you know, because the last time Jim was up in Cincinnati, well, he was pretty bad off. And naturally the doctor pulled him off. So I'm just sitting waiting, hoping and praying that when George gets back, he'll have some real good news for me. But in the meantime, I've been trying to find a day job somewhere and it's the hardest thing in the world to get a hold of anywhere. So I've been going up at the Roosevelt Hotel and I went up there Monday of this week and fella told me to come back this morning. So I went back up there this morning and he told me to check with him every day this week. And he said he's more than sure that he'll have something for me by the end of the week. Well, I do want to know, I just want something just to keep things going and, you know, to keep me from worrying too much about my expenses, you know, because when you're out of work, Bill, everything is going and nothing coming in. And it's really pretty tough on a man, particularly like my wife is now. She's been suffering with eyes and I had to take her several times to her eye specialist. Well, her medicine comes pretty high and the doctors fear it comes pretty high.
What medical expenses are.

So you know how medical expenses are, they're really high. Well, she's been doing pretty good, thank God. And I hope when I leave this time I won't have a worry on my mind like it was the last time because I really was worried about it because it was just beginning to start and I didn't know what the consequences was going to be.
Well, while I think of it, I keep interrupting, I know you were related, you are related to Johnny St. Cyr, how was, can you explain, was it?
Well, you see that was my stepfather's brother.
I knew his stepfather was something.

Yeah, you see he's my stepfather's brother and naturally my stepfather brought me up from a child about six months or a year old. So I always just consider him as a father and Johnny St. Cyr as an uncle, see? And you heard about him losing his wife?
Yes.
You heard about that?
I think you all was up there at the time when it happened, didn't you? No, it's been about a year now though.
Yeah.
Since she left that.
Well, last time I wrote to him, I wrote to him in 1957 from Frisco. But he's another one that's a very poor hand at writing anybody.
Well, I was going to ask you too, I never did talk to you about, did you play with Earl Hines? Did you stay out there?
I stayed with Earl Hines for six weeks.
I didn't remember, you see I didn't hear, I never did hear any details about that.

Yeah, well I stayed with them for six weeks at the hangover. At the hangover. Yeah, but you see my type of drumming didn't suit them any too much because I was more on the authentic side. The old style, yeah. And he wanted, Doc wanted to drum like these Dixieland drummers, so the style like Earl Hines played, you know? Well, there was no hard feelings between us because Doc had told me, he said, well, he said this thing is not definite before I went out there, you see? So I said, well, I'll take it if it's just for a month anyhow. Yeah. And I said, well, you get somebody to replace me, I'll come right on back home. So George wasn't doing nothing at the time and just like I told him, I said, well, George, I said I need some money. I got a little chance to pick up a little change by Doc for a few weeks, you know? Well, that was before they went back out there.
Who else was in the band?
Well, when I was with them, it was Earl Hines, Donnell Howard, Ed Garland, and what's this white trumpet player's name? Muggsy?
No, not Muggsy, no.
Marty Marcella?
Marty Marcella. Oh, he was there. Yeah.
And, well, it was six of us. Who was the trombone?
And Jimmy Archie.
He was there last year, I heard him. Yeah, yeah, he's still with them, yeah.
Well, Pop Foster's with them now and I think Muggsy Spang is with them now.

Well, they're still holding now. You see, Doc had wanted a house band. Well, we couldn't take it over because we had, George had too many commitments that was taken to different places at the time that Doc wanted us there. Well, naturally he just gave it up and got oil, you know? And Ed had wrote to me and told me that Doc had wanted a house band and he wanted to use me on the drums. So Doc called me up along the distance and asked me if I would take it. He said, now, it's not anything definite. He said, but if you want to take it, I said, well, you let me know right tonight and I'll send you transportation and all. So I told him, yeah, I'd take it for a few weeks, you know? And so showing up, I went on out, he sent my transportation and I went on out there. It was in 1955 in August and we opened up on Labor Day night.
That long ago, 55?
Yeah, 1955.
Almost five years.
And so I went on out there and I worked with him for six weeks. And so finally Doc found a drummer boy named Earl Watkins.
You're almost the same name.
Yeah, well, it wasn't the same name, but his first name was different than mine.
That's all I wondered, you know? I thought maybe some mistake that you really weren't there. I didn't know if you were there with him.

Yeah, I was there with him. And so Doc gave him my money and all. And so I came on down to Los Angeles. Well, I had put Saeed in my place before I left, see? I had to ship my drums off to New Orleans. And I stopped at the Beverly Cabin the night that they was working there. So Saeed asked me if I wanted my job back. I said, Saeed, I didn't come back here to look for my job back. I said, I'm just passed through on my way home. He said, well, you know, I'm in the civil service and my wife got a letter for me and wanted me to come on back home so I can go to work. I said, well, I said, you speak to George about that. So when they got off on the next intermission, he, George, and I, we went back in the restroom. We talked things over. So I told him, yeah, I said, well, George, you satisfied? I said, I'm tickled to death. So I had to rush, get in the rush there to check my drums and come to find out there was, had done got to Louisiana. So I had to pay $40 to have him ship back to Los Angeles. And so I sold him my, my ticket half fare. See, I told him, well, give me $25 and I said, you can have the ticket. So I've been back with the band ever since then, since 1955. But they can slow it up out there and this is a slow up here. The Beverly cabin closed down.
Yeah, that's what I hear. They closed.

And, uh, I think Joe Darinsburg is playing at some other place that this fellow opened up. It says quite a small place. It's not as big as the Beverly cabin, but, uh, they seem to be doing pretty good. The 400 is not open. Like they said, no, I think the 400 is open with Teddy Buckner. I think Teddy Buckner is back there. So, uh, I don't know what's what I, I haven't been writing out there for quite a while. Was a friend of ours, one of our fans I write to all the time. She always let me know, send me clippings of what's happening and all, you know. And so I'm gonna write to her one day this week and find out what's going on out there. Everybody want us out there, but, uh, the problem is to get a job somewhere else out there because that transportation problem was pretty tough on them fellas, you know what I mean, Bill? You see that, uh, take the band direct from here to, uh, California is a big price.
About a hundred and twenty dollars a piece for a railroad fare.

That's right. It's a big price, you see. So if they could, uh, combine about three or four different engagements out there like concerts or something like that, you know, and then we can go right on into the club after the concerts. It's finished like we did before. You see, but the way it is now, it's pretty tough. Cause a lot of them plants out there, airplane plants, are closed up. And that's a lot of people that's been laid off from work and they haven't been doing anything to be able to go to where it's going and where they have a good time like they want to.
Yeah.

So we just sitting back and waiting and hoping that's all we can do. And I just hope and trust the God that something will break in, huh? Even if we ever do have to go back across the water to work as long as it's working.
Yeah. Did you enjoy that trip last year?

Oh, I had a wonderful, most enjoyable time I ever had in my life. I was kind of leery, you know, because you sit down and look at television and see different things about what's going to happen over there. And you hear the news about different things that's going on. Well, I stuck close with the band. Sure. Yeah, none of them, the only man that got around was Joe Robichaud. He about the only man that, you know, revealed away from the band going around the city and all that. He tried several times to get me to go out with him. I said, no, Joe. I said, thank you very much. But I think I prefer to stay here because I have to look after drag anyhow. And if I go anywhere drag, it's going to be world half to death, you know.
Yeah. You had a lot of cold weather there too, I guess. Oh, plenty of cold weather.

But it wasn't as bad in London. It was real cold but no snow. Very little snow they had. But after we left then and went over into Europe and went to Sweden, I never seen so much snow. Good God Almighty, they had some snow over there. Jesus. Well, Copenhagen was dry, practically dry. There was no snow but it was cold. It was a dry cold but it was a wonderful place. Yeah. And I must say I really enjoyed myself over there in Copenhagen. And people were just as nice over there to us as if we was a Danish ourself, you know what I mean? Yeah. They really showed us a wonderful time and looking forward to seeing us all come back again. But every time I hear from them they all ask me about Jim and Howard. Well, I just don't know what the devil would say to them about it because…
Yeah, I know how you feel.

I wouldn't want them to think that the fellas, you know, just quit the band that's dropping on the store or something like that. So, I said, well, I just won't mention nothing about them. Just tell them I saw them and they're doing nicely and how things is here, you know, and that's all.

I was going to ask a few more questions. Yeah, go ahead. One thing, you're left-handed of course. I guess you were always… Always was left-handed. You're right-left-handed and eat left-handed. Right-left-handed, eat…
I do everything left-handed. Left-handed. Left-handed.
I'm ashamed to say, I don't remember now, the foot on your base…
I used my left foot.
You used the left foot. I don't even know.
Left foot.
Yeah, I used my left foot. I should have seen that, but I don't know.
You see my snare drum sits on the right-hand side.
I knew that. But I forgot if you used your left foot, I could use your dits. No, no.
I used my left foot.
Left foot.
You see, not my right.
I used my left foot. Does that seem more natural?
Yeah, it does. Yeah, it does.
It seems more natural. If you had to use your right foot, could you do it, do you think?
I'd have to take about six months practice to get accustomed to it, yeah.

Because some musicians, I know they count with their left foot, like when I used to play violin, I'd count with my left foot as much as the right, I think. Uh-huh. So I thought maybe it'd be just as easy for you to use your right foot.
No, no, I'd have to practice about three or four months. Just to line that over. Yeah. Because see when I started, I started with my left foot.
Yeah.
I never used my right foot for even a saxophone, because I never used a saxophone. You know a hi-hat?
Yeah, sure, I know.
Well I never used it. I just stayed, I started out authentic, I said well I'm going to stay authentic.
Yeah.
And I got so accustomed to using that left foot. See I never, see I don't play like some drummers like that from the heel. See how it gets it from here.
You use it from almost from your hip. See I'm on my toes.
Yeah.
Like that, see.

You don't keep your heel down on the- No, my heel very, unless I'm playing a slow number, while I'm on my toes like that, then I relax it with my heel, see. Yeah. Go right like that, you know. Then I'm relaxing with my heel and I don't feel it. And when I knock off, I never feel my leg don't feel tired or nothing like that, you know. Because I feel good. Some of the drummers, you see where they're catching that is right up here in this ankle. On the ankle, yeah. See right here. Mm-hmm. That's why you catch a lot of them is only hitting a one beat on a fast number. And when they slow down the tempo, then they can get that tempo, you know, from the ankle.
Yeah, baby used to have to do that and after you had it, you couldn't move it fast.

No, I noticed that because he had wrestled me up several times at the hunt club in Chicago. He used to come there and ask about the wrestling up. I said, man, I said, you're doing me all the good in the world. I said, they sit out in that audience and look at you sitting up on my drums. I said, it makes me feel good, baby. One night I cried, I'm telling you the truth. I really broke down and cried, you know, to see how he was up there fighting, you know, to try to get his arms in shape, you know. And I said, well, that just look like that's going to be it. Yeah, the second time he had come to that club when we was playing there. And George told him, George, well, Lawrence was living there. That was the last time Lawrence played out there with us. Lawrence said, brother Lawrence, I don't know. He said, but he said, our boy look like he's gone. I said, yeah, I believe so too. I said, because he can't get his wrist to work and right, you know. I said, it's kind of slowing him up because George was playing practically all slow numbers. He didn't play nothing fast, but he played practically all slow numbers so he could keep up the tempo. But he told me, he said, Joe, I ain't going to be able to make it anymore. He said, I'm trying. He said, I've got several engagements coming up and he said, I'm going to do my best with them. I said, well, perhaps the best of luck to you. But I said, I do hope you can make a comeback. I said, I would like to see you make a comeback. I said, because I said, it's hard. I said, I don't know to say, I can't say how many authentic jazz drums we got living. I mean, left that's playing today. I don't know. I said, I know Paul is one. I said, and I'm counting myself. And I said, you the other one. I said, but outside of that, I don't know if there are others.
I said, very few.
I mean, authentic jazz drummers like we play.

Well, I was going to ask if you ever knew Snaggs Jones. Snaggs? Snaggs they called him. I can't think of his first name now. He went to Chicago and played with Joe Oliver, but he came from here. He was left handed. Snaggs Jones.
He used to throw the sticks around.
He didn't, you know, a lot of that fancy stuff. Like Black Benny used to do, yeah. The Black Benny used to have a snare stick there? Yeah, you see, Black Benny started that, yeah.
Well, I never did follow that style with being fancy because.
No, I know, but I just thought maybe you saw this left handed drummer though. You don't remember him.
No, I don't remember him, no.
Do you remember any other left handed drummers from New Orleans?
None other than Henry Morton.
Oh, Henry Morton. I didn't know, he was. Yeah, he was left handed too.
I forgot if I knew it.
Yeah, he was left handed. He was left handed. I didn't know.

Did he use his left foot then too? Used his left foot too. That's practically where I got my learning from because he was learning me, you know, and he asked me what way I wanted to set up. So I set up left handed. And that's how I started out, playing left handed. I can't even right left handed. I can't stir apart left handed. I mean right handed. Yeah, I know what you mean. I got to use my left hand for practically everything. You see I'm handicapped a little bit that way, you know, because a lot of times I want to use my right hand for something and I don't know, this seems so awkward. I just get light on doing it with my left hand.

Yeah, a lot of things are made for right handed people too. Yeah, that's right. Some tools and things are made that way. That's right. This tape is just about out. We'll let this run out. Yeah, okay. Things are real. . . .
Is there anything else you can say about the left handed drumming?

Well I don't know, not anything too much, but lots of people, it has them puzzled about how I play. They want to know how I'm set up. I say well I'm set up for a left hand style. They say well how do you do for, see I see some drummer look like they got that snare drum right in front of the bass drum. I say well that's them bop players. I say how in the world they can get a chance to kick their bass drum I don't know. But I say they do it and I say they keep their snares down which gives the snare drum a kind of a dead beat. But I say that's the way they supposed to be playing but I don't, I say I just don't get the tempo of it. I say there don't seem to be a beat in it. But they all want to know about my left handed playing. I say well that's the way I play. I say it looks so awkward. The way you playing with things over here and we used to sing with drummers with everything on this side. I say sometimes it really looks awkward to me. I say I can say I look at a right hand drum and I say I just imagine that his drum should be on the right hand side. And I say it really seems awkward. And that's the way Henry Martin used to play also. I used to watch him and I say that's, the last time when I was going to school I started the right with my left hand. See I just started right off left handed. I never do nothing with my right hand. I just started right off left handed and I just kept it up. The old folks they didn't try to correct me with it through right hand or nothing like that. So I just went right on to it and I got so accustomed to it it would be a task to change it.
You mentioned about some of the modern drummers and bop drummers having a dead beat on the bass drum.
Yeah they keeps that uh uh uh their snares down. You see their heads is tight but they keeps their snares off which gives it that fuel uh uh
almost like muffled drums.
Yeah that's right.
I wondered about the bass drum. Um would you say that most of the old timers had used the bass drum more? Was it a bigger louder tone than the modern kids? It had a louder tone.
It had a louder tone and it wasn't much work. If you get what I mean you didn't have to hit too hard. Because you could just do like that and you get that boom sign off it like Baby Dodds drums.
Yeah I know how he played it.
Because you notice he had that big drum there and he didn't have to hit hard.
No.

But he got that volume out of it though. But you see when I'm playing I got a muffler on the front of my bass drum on the left hand side and by me kicking the way I do it because George likes playing the bass drum. You see I have to kick pretty hard. Yeah. But you see when I first started playing with George I used to play a heel and toe until we started back at Manus Tavern and he told me and said Joe I'm going to have to get you out of that. He said because I can't hardly hear that bass drum. Well mine was a much smaller bass drum that would be able to die because it was a 24. Well you couldn't get much volume out of sitting down there hitting it from heel to toe. So he said, I said what you want me to do? He said well you get a high stool and he said that'll put you right on your toes. Well I was rather puzzled. I said now I don't know if I'm going to be able to make this beat right like that you know. So the following week I borrowed a stool from the ball. And sure enough I got a good volume out of bass drum as small as it was and I've been playing like that ever since.
How big is your bass drum now?
Mine is a 24.
But it's still the same one.
Yeah that case is a 28. That's a 28 inch case and my bass drum is a 24.
Did most of the old time drummers that you heard like Henry Martin and 2 Bits and all those pedals had pretty big drums? Yeah.
All of them. Right there all because they wasn't making no small type bass drum during them days. Did they hit it pretty hard?
I mean was there a lot of more bass drums?
Oh it got pretty volume out of them because them overhanging pedals really hit.
More than the modern drummers do. Yeah.
And then besides that you had a side cymbal.
Oh yeah I was going to ask about that. Yeah you had a side cymbal.
Did you ever use one of those?
Yeah.
When my first set I bought from Wetherless I had the overhanging pedal and a side cymbal I had on the left hand side.
Every time you hit the bass drum it did.
They both hit at the same time and then when you want to you just take your stick and just throw it off and wouldn't hear nothing but the bass drum.
I remember that.
Well I used to watch Baby Dots do that you know and that's where I learned that from him because I used to watch him when he used to play up on the old Temple roof garden.
Oh yeah.

He used to play up there many times and I used to watch him at old Kenny's Hall on Padilla Street when he'd get to act about two or three choruses you know then he'd throw that off and all you would hear was that bass drum and snare drum going. Because Baby Dots I never saw him use a hi-hat.
No I don't think he ever did.

He never did like them. No he never did like them. And I bought one and I tried and George told me, he said, George said, if you're going to stick to authentic jazz you don't need no hi-hat. He said, just your snare drum, bass drum, cymbal and your tum tum and wood block is all you need. I said, well thank God for that because I was about to buy jungle drums and every other doggone thing. He said, no you don't need all that stuff with it. He said, we just go stick with this authentic jazz and he said, we make our name on that. And sure enough we did. And I was sitting down inside the other day saying to myself, I said, well, I said, I've been cut quite a few records with him and I said, my name will be, will last as long as his will. I said, we may be dead and gone, but, but I do believe as long as the world stand, we'll, our name will be mentioned. I said, that's a whole lot of glory to a man, but that, that's actually glory come to you after you're dead, not while you're living. Yeah, that's right.
Often it happens. Yeah.

Often it happens that way. Now you see, they ain't said much about baby Dutch yet, but in the near future you go hear a lot of talk about him. See, you don't hear all anybody saying nothing now, but you never can, can tell what's going to come up later on.
No. Did you ever hear a few of the other drummers I'll ask you about, like Old Man Cottrell, we were talking about his stuff earlier?

Well, yeah, yeah, I heard Old Man Cottrell, I see him every week at the Old Lyric Theatre, because he was playing out there with the, not the, not the, but the, Kimball, a trumpet player. Mm-hmm. Well, he used to play out there with them when they was having vaudeville out there. At the Lyric. At the Old Lyric Theatre, yeah. And, uh, what, Black Benny?
Well, tell me something more about Black Benny, because I never got to hear him or see him. I don't know.
Well, he was a wonderful drummer and he was a great showman. It's a pity that he died the way he did, but he really was a great showman.
Armstrong talks a lot about him. Yeah. Yeah, that's right. I wondered, did he do mostly brass band work or dance?
He did both. He did both. He did both. Dance band and brass band. And he, well, in the brass band he used to play bass drum.
Mm-hmm.

And he played the traps they used to call them in them days. Yeah. In dance bands, you know, and he played at the Lyric's for a while and after Old Man Cottrell left and, uh, very happy he played out there for a while. Well, he was another one that didn't, uh, didn't know how to read. I don't think either one of them read music.
What style did he play, if you can tell anything about it? Red Happy, was he?

Well, Red Happy wasn't no fancy drummer. He was more on the straight type. Straight type. He was something similar to Old Man Cottrell. He tried to keep the beat in there, you know, like Old Man Cottrell used to do. He never would say fancy, he'd hit on the bass drum like I, like you hear me do sometime and play the wood blocks and play on the cymbal and all that, but he was really a wonderful drummer. And I think he learned, I think Henry Martin learned Black Benny how to play. But that fancy stuff, Black Benny taking that up himself. Mm-hmm. See? He was going great guns when he got killed. See, he got killed by some woman from the band.
I heard about that.

In the third ward and, uh, well that was the end of him. And I've never seen a funeral in my life like he had. I think they had about three or four bands. Really? Yeah. And on top of the hoist, well that's before they started using these limousines. They were using horses at that time. And on top of the hoist, they had his bass drum up there. His real drum. His real bass drum. Yeah, his real bass drum. And they had it up on top of the hoist. And I'll never forget it. I saw him at Canal and Claiborne. We was turning Canal into Claiborne going into the St. Louis St. Cemetery. Well he's buried over there. Yeah, he's buried in one of them cemeteries there. I didn't have time to see which one it was because I was going to work at the time, you know? And that's where they buried him out there in one of them cemeteries. No, Mr. He's out there?
No. I think it's back in Gentilly. Mount Olivet I believe.

Oh yes, that's where Stella stands. Yeah, Mount Olivet I think he's buried. I think they're taking him as far as Biennival and Galvis. And that's where the bands left the funeral. Take him on out there. But that's where they had his bass drum. I've never seen a funeral for no musician like that since. Trumpet, flares, trombone, flares, and nobody else. They really honored him. They really honored him a great deal.
But he's been very popular.
Oh, he was a popular man. And what the people liked about him, he was what you say a protector. If he was with you and somebody wanted to make a little trouble for you, he was right there with you.
That's what Armstrong says too. He may have been a little bit tough, but he helped me out and keep you out. Yeah, he was right there with you. And he didn't take nothing off of nobody.
Not off of anybody, not off the policemen. And the police in them days was men alongside what we have today.
That's so, yes.

We got mostly youngsters now dead, but when I was a kid coming up, you had policemen way up in their age that had been on the force for years. And they knew how to treat people. But black men didn't worry about nobody. And then he just had to go get killed by that woman. He got killed by her and somebody killed her. Well that was that.
Do you know any bands that he played with in the ...

Well in them days I think it was the Eureka. Oh, I forget the name of the brass band he was playing with. But it was one of the old standard brass bands. Yeah. It was either the Eureka or the Excelsa brass band. I don't think they're in existence anymore, the Excelsa brass band.
No. Any of the dance orchestra that you ever heard him with?
Well I never heard him play with no other band outside of Old Man Joe Robichaux.
Joe Robichaux.

Yeah, and he was playing at the Old Leryx Theater. That's the only band I've ever heard him play with. And he was really the whole show himself. A lot of people went there, most would see him, not to see the actors on the stage, most would see him perform. Cause he really was a wonderful show.
Down in the pit too.

Right down in the pit, that's right down in the pit. Cause I had the first seat right up there by the pit, you know. I just leaned right on the rear like that and just looked right at him. And I used to go, that's where I used to sit all the time. I always made sure I got there early enough to get that seat. And that's where I used to sit and I used to watch him and I used to watch Red Happer there too. But I never seen Happer outside of the pit playing dance band. Oh yeah, when he was playing with Kid Horry. Oh yeah. He used to play with Kid Horry at the old Pelican dance hall, which was on Gravy near Rampart, right at the corner. Oh sure, I know. Yeah, right upstairs on the second floor. Yeah. Well that's the only dance place that I knew Red Happer to play with a band outside of the Lyrics Theatre with old man Joe Robe show. And he, he done some pretty good work. Cause when I was playing out at the Beverly Cabin before Ory, first time we went out there. And Ory came by to see us after we taken the job over, you know, because he was taking off for a while. I think he was going off somewhere, I'll just forget now. But anyhow, he came up and told me, say, you know, you remind me of Henry Martin and Red Happer. I said, I do. He said, yeah, you see, I like your style of playing. I said, well, I say, you know, I'm from the old Third Ward too. He said, you're from the Third Ward. I said, that's right, down in New Orleans. He said, I thought it was something mighty familiar about that beat you had there. But you see that beat I got, Bill, let me show you how some fellas, yes. You see, I learned from two or three different drummers. Now that beat I have, that fast tempo, I got that from Zutty Singleton.
I was going to ask if you saw Zutty, he used to beat the lyric too.

Yeah, yeah, but I wasn't going there at that time when he was there. But I used to watch him on different advertisements. You know, he used to play on the truck, you know. And I used to listen to his beat all the time. I said, I don't see how that man don't get tired beating like that. Until George told me, he said, that's how Zutty used to beat. This is the way I'm showing you. He said, you can get a faster beat and you won't feel half as tired as if you get it played from the ankle. And he wasn't telling no lie because I never felt tired when I knocked off. I don't care how hard we worked or how long of hours we worked. The only job that killed me was out there on Bourbon Street. On them dead nights bill, I was just as dead as the nights were. Because when you don't have nobody around, you know, to sit down and applaud or ask you for different numbers or something like that or smile up at you, it just kills your spirit. But like on concert, we play at different concerts, man, we get all them applaud shots. I'm ready to kill myself then. See, because I know the people that's enjoying it and they're making me feel good to see they enjoying it. But you catch a dead house, you just don't have no spirit to play nothing. Not even a piano or clarinet or anything. But when the people start to give you applause and hoorah and all like that, well, you're ready to give them a nice work. You ain't gonna worry about the hours passing in. But you sit out there on Bourbon Street up on them bandstand and catch dead nights. You wanna know every time you could be looking at that clock to see what time it is. And that's where I used to be out there and we was working out there. And then with some tough hours, six hours a night. Yeah. It's really hard hours. If you had somewhere to go for them and your break is so short, you don't have time to go nowhere to get, you know, to sit down and just the band sitting back there talking. Well, you wanna be somewhere where you can sit down and talk with different people, you know, or something like that. But we didn't have no chance to do anything like that out there because they brought us out on the sidewalk when we was playing at the Amaraka. They wouldn't let us come out there. We used to go out there on intermission to catch a little fresh air. The police told the provider to keep us off of the sidewalk. But we wasn't working nobody but ourselves.

You know, I've heard that they did that too. Yeah. Still, I have seen a couple of musicians sometimes would go up and hear another band outside like Paul Barber and you're playing. Yeah, you could do that, yeah. Or somebody would go up and hear another band.
Because when we was working at Mardi Gras, Bill and them used to come down and listen to us and we used to go down and listen to them, you know.
The pad out there.
Yeah, when Paul was out there we used to go over there and listen to him too, you know, and they'd come by us and listen.
It's hard to have time and 15 minutes to get there.

If you don't have no time, no time to go nowhere. Time was too short. They let you play for it and take a 20 minute break where when you get back on the bandstand you feel like working. But 15 minutes, it takes you almost five minutes to get back to the dressing room. Because this one stopped you, that one stopped you, you know, and talking about different things. First thing you know it's almost time to get back up on the bandstand.
You remember another old time drummer, Zeno, Henry Zeno. Henry Zeno.

Yeah, now wait now, that name is familiar now, Henry Zeno. I'm trying to think who I used to hear him play with. Henry Zeno. Oh, I just can't come back to him now. In fact, I never did word with going around him too much because he wasn't playing that regular.
Yeah, and you weren't a drummer at that time hardly I guess. No, no. He must have quit pretty early.
Yeah, he did quit pretty early.
I think he was with the Eagle band some part of the time. Yeah. Maybe Joe Oliver and Bunk and people like that way back.
That was way back a long time. That was before I started to go at the dances.
Another old timer, probably before your time, Chandler.
Chandler? Yeah.
Do you remember him?
I don't remember him, no.
He'd been with Robichaux and bands way back.
Yeah, no, I don't remember him. Do you remember him? No. I might have his picture in my insight.
What about Walter Grundy? That was one of Baby's teachers. Do you remember him?
No, but I've heard of him, but I don't know him personally. I've heard a lot of him.
Another fella Baby talked about was Mac Murray.
Mac Murray.
Supposed to have a little banjo head for his snare drum, you know, a real banjo head.
Oh yeah, uh-huh.
Without the, just one side, snare. Oh yeah.
Yeah, well I've never heard of him, but I've saw those snare drums. Yeah, I saw those style, those single-head snare drums. Did they have any tone?
I can't imagine. They had a nice tone. They had a nice volume to them, yeah.

They had a nice volume to them. But I, when I started playing they had to cut out using them. And, well in them days you used to, you was able to go to a pawn shop, we didn't have no drums, you was able to go to a pawn shop and rent a set. Okay. They charge you a dollar for the whole outfit for one night.
Right.

Well that's, I copied that from Happi because Happi used to do that really. Happi used to do that all the time, you know. And, well he wanted to go to a dance. He even went and rented the snare drum so he could get in the dance without paying, you know, because he was charging admission at the door. Well he carried the snare drum along with him and this letter went right on. He just went up on the bandstand and get up there and set the drum up a while, you know, rest him up and, well I started doing the same doggone thing, you know. So I used to, and I used to carry Joe Lynch's drums for him too.
Well I can ask more about Joe Lynch's.

And I used to get into different dances with him, you know, carrying a snare drum for him. Well at them times they didn't have no bass drum case of any kind then. Yeah. You carried the bass drum on your back and you had a little sack made for your snare drum and assembly sticks and your overhanging pedal and all that in there, you know. But nowadays you got to have a case because this traveling, you never make it on the road like that.
Well, what about Joe Lindsey? How did he play and who did he play with? Do you remember much about that?

Well, Joe Lindsey was playing down on Claiborne between Quarntire and St. Louis. They had a dance hall there in them days. And he was playing with Kid Ory. Well Louis played down there for a while too, before you know, before he went out there on the boat. Well it was Joe, it was Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory, Lorenzo Teo, Joe Lindsey. I forgot who else he had with him. But they didn't have no piano. He had seven men. They wasn't using no piano. They was using a saxophone and banjo, clarinet, trumpet, trombone, drums, bass.
I met Joe Lindsey once in Chicago and then he came back here. I never met him here later, but I know he didn't play much in late years.
No, no, he had given up drums and joined the church and he had joined some youth center before he died.
Oh, is that it?
I didn't know what happened. Yeah, because he was working out there on Bourbon Street somewhere.
I think at the Absinthe House, I think he was at the border. Yeah, somewhere around there, yeah.

I heard that. Because he used to pass by and stop and talk with us every night when he was going to work and out there and got to work. He used to pass by all the time and stop and talk with us. He was a real good drummer. He was a real good drummer.
I had another question I was going to ask.
They shoot it right off.
I lost my paper.
Oh gosh.
One thing about the district, can you remember anything more? Here it is. Anything more about the music and the district when you were a porter?

Well, when I was working around there, Bill, I wasn't allowed in them places because I was too young at that time because I was just like I said I was 13 years old. And even when I got to be 16 years old, I wasn't allowed in them places, in the dance halls at night, you know.
Yeah.

Because police was pretty strict on youngsters out there in them days. You see anybody just side of Claiborne Street that was in short pants couldn't venture across Claiborne between Iverville to St. Louis to go in town. You either had to go around St. Louis Street or go out Canal Street. You couldn't pass through the old Tenderloin District.
Couldn't walk through there.

Couldn't walk through there at all unless you was with some of your parents. There was the only way you could get through there. But see what made me go in short pants or long pants so early? We was living on Marais between Cornelis and St. Louis. Well, that was a part of the old Tenderloin District. So the police didn't advise my mother to get me a pair of long pants or either she'd have to move out.
Yeah.

So my uncle gave me my first pair of long pants to go to, and I went to work the following week. Frederick Brown had wanted the bellhop and I went to work around there working at night from 2 in the evening to 2 in the morning. I worked 12 hours during them days around there. Yeah. But he was making money. But the night shifts were the best because that's when everything was opening up and all the, you know, spokesmen coming through that going to different houses and that's where we used to make our money. It wasn't nothing in the daytime because practically everybody was asleep.
You see?
So I made pretty good money. My salary was four and a half a week. But I was pulling down over. I'm about $35 and $40 in them days a week. I'm about to get a little bit of a job. Excuse my salary.
Yeah.
But I was a child, well I gave it all to my parents.
I wondered if you ever got into any of the houses like Lula White's or anything to hear any of the piano players?
Well, no, in through the back. You never could go through the front.
You never did get to hear the piano? No.

I never did see what the front part looked like. I've always heard what it looked like but I never got in the front. And I used to go by old Emma Johnson. She had the old play step right next to the fire engine house that used to be out there. I was on Basin and Corn Eye. Well, I used to say the front was given out on Basin Street side and I used to have to go through the back on Franklin Street.
You see?
Well, in fact, all them houses around there was given out on the front but the back gave out to Franklin.
Yeah.

Well, we never did all that thing where we used to have to go through the back. You see? But the only place that we was able to go into the front was like these little cribs like, you know? Yeah. You didn't have to go through no alley, nothing. Just stop right outside to the front and just pass the stuff through the door and collect your money and that was it.
Somebody told me once that Emma Johnson had what you might call a circus house, you know, a lot of extra stunts and shows and all that. She did.
That's true, isn't it? Yeah, she did. Yeah, she was well known for that.
Yeah.
You know, Willie P. I said she was another one. She used to put on those stunts once in a while.
She did too. I didn't know about it.
But Emma Johnson put them on more than anybody else around there, you know? I didn't get a chance of peeping on one of the shows and I said I never want to see
any more of them.

It was terrible. Well I see them big rich men, Bill, used to come there, they paid $50, $100 a head to see them kind of thing. They come in a group, they call it Self Out On A Good Time, slumming they call it, and they call it some money for that one night slumming. Yeah. Well, in them days you had rough top beer that was selling for $0.05 a pint bottle. A quart was $0.50. Budweiser beer was selling for $0.50, we used to charge them a dollar. The rough top bottle beer was $0.05, we would charge them a quarter. Well see that money, we used to work that with them women out there, you know? They'd give them that price and then we'd divvy up after everything was over and they was ready to turn in. Well we'd go around and collect our little divvy, you know, and they'd take the other half, you see? Well that's where you made your money. It wasn't so much on the tips. But when you got any good with them people out there and you work up a deal, well they used to catch most of them fell what they used to call chummies off the ship. You see? Well that's where we used to work them deals with them.
Were they just ordinary sailors or what that came out of the ship?
Well, regular sailors and seamen. Sailors and seamen.
Mr. Bell, you want to answer that?

Yeah, that ain't for me, that's where they grow up in there. That's on the two rings. They used to work that on the sailors and seamen. And they used to, well, they'd never, see like at night time they never order canned beer. Because canned beer was too cheap. Yeah.
I didn't know they had canned beer in those days, did they?

Oh yeah. You get a regular, we had regular cans about that high, about that big around. You get a half a can of beer for a nickel. You fill it up for a dime. They used to sell wine the same way. Get a half a can of wine for a nickel. Well they call it Sweet Lucy because they had syrup put in and they give it the name of Sweet Lucy.
Yeah.

The other women get out there in Harlem and say, bring me a half a can of Sweet Lucy. Well you know what that meant? There was a wine, clavard wine or port wine and syrup. But in the daytime, now that was in the daytime, but at nighttime was nothing but bottled beer, no wine. Everything was bottled beer.
Yeah.
Because they was charging a higher price for it. But if a guy had had sex, he wanted to drink a beer, he'd go in the bar room and get it over the bar, he'd get it for a nickel. Yeah.

You see? Well do you remember, was there a place, Turo's, that had lunches or something? Food, was that a restaurant? Do you remember that? Turo's. I think that was at Conti, wasn't it? Turo's. Bienville, I guess. They called it Bienville and Basin.
Oh, Bienville and Basin? Yeah.
Oh, I never had much contact.
You never got up in there.
I thought you might have gone there.
No, like Tom Anderson and that place. I never got up Tom Anderson's?
No. You never got up Tom Anderson's?

No. I never got that far. The farthest I went was to Franklin, back to Robinson. Yeah. And from, I'd say from St. Louis to Iberville. That was the first, that was our locale, you know, because they didn't allow you to go around in front of them houses.
Were there many of the good houses back there, away from Basin Street, back in the-

No, the good houses mostly out there. On Basin. Around Basin Street. And they had a few on the other side of Ramport Street. Yeah. Between Ramport and Burgundy. I used to have a few around there. On there too.
Were they mostly cribs then, just the individual?

Well, no, all the cribs was this side, but them was mostly apartment houses like, you know. Well, people lived in there then. Oh yeah, they lived in there, but those prostitutes, you know. Yeah. Well, they lived in there and that's where they did all their business, right out there.
Yeah.
